en: Hi, I don't think we have met. I'm Karthik.
tamil: ஹாய், நாம சந்திச்சதில்லன்னு நினைக்கிறேன். நான் கார்த்திக்.
context: Introducing yourself to a stranger at a party.
explain: 'I don't think we have met' is a polite way to start talking to someone new.
usage: Use it at a party or function when you want to introduce yourself to someone.
leelaQ: How do you start a talk with a new person at a party?
answer: I say hi and tell my name with a smile.

en: Nice to meet you. I have heard a lot about you.
tamil: உங்களை சந்திச்சதுல சந்தோஷம். உங்களைப் பத்தி நிறைய கேள்விப்பட்டிருக்கேன்.
context: Meeting a friend's relative for the first time.
explain: 'I have heard a lot about you' is a warm line that makes the other person feel good.
usage: Say it when a friend or colleague introduces you to someone new.
leelaQ: What do you say when a friend introduces you to his family?
answer: I say nice to meet you and smile.

en: Which part of Tamil Nadu is your family from?
tamil: உங்க குடும்பம் தமிழ்நாட்டுல எந்தப் பகுதி?
context: Making small talk with a new neighbour.
explain: This question asks about someone's family roots in a friendly way.
usage: Ask it to a new acquaintance when you want to start a friendly chat.
leelaQ: Which part of your state is your family from?
answer: My family is from the Coimbatore side.

en: Please come in and make yourself at home.
tamil: தயவு செஞ்சு உள்ள வாங்க, உங்க வீடு மாதிரி நினைச்சுக்கோங்க.
context: Welcoming guests at your front door.
explain: 'Make yourself at home' means feel free and comfortable here.
usage: Say it to guests when they enter your house for the first time.
leelaQ: How do you welcome guests who come to your house?
answer: I open the door, smile and ask them to sit down.

en: Thank you so much for inviting us tonight.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு எங்களை கூப்பிட்டதுக்கு ரொம்ப நன்றி.
context: Thanking the host at a dinner party.
explain: 'Thank you for' is followed by an -ing word: inviting, helping, coming.
usage: Say it to the host when you arrive or when you leave a party.
leelaQ: Did you thank the host the last time you went to a party?
answer: Yes, I thanked the host before I left.

en: The food was delicious, especially the biryani.
tamil: சாப்பாடு ரொம்ப சுவையா இருந்துச்சு, குறிப்பா பிரியாணி.
context: Praising the food at a friend's house.
explain: 'Especially' points to the one thing you liked the most.
usage: Say it to the host after a meal to make them happy.
leelaQ: What was the best dish you ate at a party?
answer: The best dish I ate was my aunt's chicken biryani.

en: Can I get you something to drink?
tamil: உங்களுக்கு குடிக்க ஏதாவது எடுத்துட்டு வரட்டுமா?
context: Offering a drink to a guest at home.
explain: 'Can I get you...?' is a friendly way to offer something to a guest.
usage: Use it when a guest or visitor comes to your home or table.
leelaQ: What do you offer a guest when he comes home?
answer: I offer him tea or cold water first.

en: Sorry, could you tell me your name once more?
tamil: மன்னிச்சிடுங்க, உங்க பேரை இன்னொரு தடவை சொல்றீங்களா?
context: Asking a new person to repeat their name.
explain: 'Could you' is a polite way to ask. 'Once more' means one more time.
usage: Use it when you did not hear a name clearly in a noisy place.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not hear someone's name?
answer: I politely ask the person to say the name again.

en: I'm going to leave now, it's getting late.
tamil: நான் இப்ப கிளம்பறேன், நேரமாச்சு.
context: Saying goodbye early at a party.
explain: 'Going to' shows your plan. 'Getting late' means the time is moving on.
usage: Say it to the host when you need to go home early.
leelaQ: How do you leave a party politely?
answer: I thank the host and say I have to go home early.

en: It was lovely talking to you. Let's keep in touch.
tamil: உங்ககிட்ட பேசினது ரொம்ப சந்தோஷம். தொடர்புல இருப்போம்.
context: Ending a chat with someone you just met.
explain: 'Keep in touch' means to stay in contact by phone or message.
usage: Say it at the end of a chat when you want to stay in contact.
leelaQ: How do you stay in touch with people you meet newly?
answer: I take their number and send them a message.

en: Would you like to join us for dinner on Saturday?
tamil: சனிக்கிழமை எங்களோட டின்னருக்கு வர்றீங்களா?
context: Inviting a colleague for a meal.
explain: 'Would you like to' is a polite way to invite someone.
usage: Use it to invite friends, neighbours or colleagues in a polite way.
leelaQ: Who would you like to invite for dinner this weekend?
answer: I would like to invite my close friends this weekend.

en: I'm afraid I can't make it to the party this weekend.
tamil: இந்த வாரக் கடைசி பார்ட்டிக்கு என்னால வர முடியாதுன்னு நினைக்கிறேன்.
context: Politely declining an invitation.
explain: 'I'm afraid' softens bad news. 'Make it' means to be able to come.
usage: Use it to refuse an invitation without hurting the person.
leelaQ: How do you say no to an invitation politely?
answer: I say sorry, thank them and give a short reason.

en: Happy birthday! Wishing you a wonderful year ahead.
tamil: பிறந்தநாள் வாழ்த்துகள்! வரப்போற வருஷம் அருமையா இருக்கட்டும்.
context: Wishing a friend on his birthday.
explain: 'Wishing you...' is a short form of 'I am wishing you...' used in greetings.
usage: Say it or write it in a card or message on someone's birthday.
leelaQ: How do you wish your friends on their birthday?
answer: I call them and say happy birthday with a gift.

en: Congratulations on your promotion, you really deserve it.
tamil: உங்க பதவி உயர்வுக்கு வாழ்த்துகள், நீங்க அதுக்கு தகுதியானவங்க.
context: Congratulating a colleague at work.
explain: 'Congratulations on' is followed by the good news. 'Deserve' means you earned it.
usage: Say it to a friend or colleague who has got good news or success.
leelaQ: Who got a good news recently and what did you say?
answer: My cousin got a job and I said congratulations.

en: Is anyone sitting here, or can I take this chair?
tamil: இங்க யாராவது உட்கார்ந்திருக்காங்களா, இல்ல நான் இந்த நாற்காலியை எடுத்துக்கலாமா?
context: Looking for a seat at a crowded function.
explain: This is a polite way to check before taking a seat.
usage: Use it at weddings, events or meetings when seats are limited.
leelaQ: Do you like to sit in front or at the back in a function?
answer: I like to sit at the back so I can leave easily.

en: You have a lovely house. Did you decorate it yourself?
tamil: உங்க வீடு ரொம்ப அழகா இருக்கு. நீங்களே அலங்கரிச்சீங்களா?
context: Complimenting a friend's new home.
explain: A compliment followed by a question keeps the talk going.
usage: Use it when you visit someone's house for the first time.
leelaQ: What do you notice first when you visit a new house?
answer: I notice the colour of the walls and the cleanliness.

en: Please don't trouble yourself, I'm fine with plain water.
tamil: தயவு செஞ்சு சிரமப்படாதீங்க, எனக்கு சாதாரண தண்ணியே போதும்.
context: Refusing extra effort from a host politely.
explain: 'Don't trouble yourself' tells the host not to take extra effort.
usage: Say it when a host is doing too much for you and you want to be polite.
leelaQ: What do you say when a host offers you too many things?
answer: I say thank you and that a little is enough.

en: I'll introduce you to my cousin, she also loves cooking.
tamil: என் கசினை உங்களுக்கு அறிமுகப்படுத்தறேன், அவளுக்கும் சமைக்கறது ரொம்ப பிடிக்கும்.
context: Connecting two people at a function.
explain: 'I'll introduce you to' is used to bring two people together.
usage: Use it at a family function to connect a friend with a relative.
leelaQ: Whom did you introduce to your friends recently?
answer: I introduced my brother to my college friends.

en: Do you mind if I sit with you for a while?
tamil: நான் கொஞ்ச நேரம் உங்களோட உட்கார்ந்தா பரவாயில்லையா?
context: Joining someone at a table or bench.
explain: 'Do you mind if I...' politely asks permission. Answer 'Not at all' to say yes.
usage: Use it to join a stranger's table at a canteen, wedding or function.
leelaQ: Do you like sitting alone or with other people?
answer: I like sitting with other people because I enjoy talking.

en: My wife and I will be there around seven.
tamil: நானும் என் மனைவியும் ஏழு மணி போல அங்க இருப்போம்.
context: Confirming your arrival time for a function.
explain: 'Around seven' means near seven, not exactly seven.
usage: Say it to the host when they ask if you are coming and at what time.
leelaQ: What time do you usually reach a function?
answer: I usually reach a little before the start time.

en: Thanks for dropping by, it made my day.
tamil: வந்து பார்த்ததுக்கு நன்றி, என் நாளையே சந்தோஷமாக்கிட்டீங்க.
context: Thanking a friend who visited unexpectedly.
explain: 'Dropping by' means visiting without much planning. 'Made my day' means made me very happy.
usage: Say it to a friend or relative who visits you suddenly.
leelaQ: Who visited you unexpectedly last time?
answer: My old school friend visited me last month.

en: Don't be shy, take some more snacks.
tamil: கூச்சப்படாதீங்க, இன்னும் கொஞ்சம் ஸ்நாக்ஸ் எடுத்துக்கோங்க.
context: Encouraging a guest to eat more.
explain: 'Don't be shy' is a friendly way to tell someone to feel free.
usage: Say it to guests at home who eat very little out of politeness.
leelaQ: What snacks do you give guests at your home?
answer: I give them murukku, sweets and hot tea.

en: How do you know the bride and groom?
tamil: மணமக்களை உங்களுக்கு எப்படித் தெரியும்?
context: Making conversation at a wedding.
explain: A good small-talk question for any event where people come from different sides.
usage: Ask it at a wedding to start a chat with a stranger sitting near you.
leelaQ: Whose wedding did you go to last and how did you know them?
answer: I went to my friend's wedding. We studied together in college.

en: Sorry for the late reply, I was travelling all day.
tamil: தாமதமா பதில் சொன்னதுக்கு மன்னிச்சிடுங்க, நாள் முழுக்க பயணத்துல இருந்தேன்.
context: Apologising for answering a message late.
explain: 'Sorry for' is followed by a noun. Then you can give the reason.
usage: Use it in a message or call when you could not reply on time.
leelaQ: Why do people sometimes reply late to messages?
answer: They may be busy at work or travelling.

en: Thank you so much for remembering my birthday.
tamil: என் பிறந்தநாளை நினைவுல வச்சதுக்கு ரொம்ப நன்றி.
context: Thanking a colleague who wished you.
explain: 'So much' makes the thanks stronger. 'Remembering' is the -ing form after 'for'.
usage: Say it to a friend or colleague who wished you on your birthday.
leelaQ: Who wished you first on your last birthday?
answer: My mother wished me first, early in the morning.

en: I'm so sorry, I didn't mean to hurt you.
tamil: ரொம்ப மன்னிச்சிடுங்க, உங்களை காயப்படுத்தணும்னு நான் நினைக்கலை.
context: Apologising after saying something hurtful.
explain: 'Didn't mean to' tells the person it was not your intention.
usage: Use it with friends or family when your words upset them by mistake.
leelaQ: What do you do when you hurt a friend by mistake?
answer: I say sorry and explain that I did not mean it.

en: Excuse me, you're standing on my foot.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், நீங்க என் காலை மிதிச்சிட்டு நிக்கறீங்க.
context: Politely telling someone in a crowd.
explain: 'Excuse me' is a gentle way to get attention before you complain.
usage: Use it in a bus, train or crowded temple when someone steps on you.
leelaQ: How do you speak to a stranger in a crowded bus?
answer: I say excuse me and speak in a polite voice.

en: Please forgive me for being late to your function.
tamil: உங்க விழாவுக்கு தாமதமா வந்ததுக்கு என்னை மன்னிச்சிடுங்க.
context: Apologising to a host for arriving late.
explain: 'Forgive me for' is followed by an -ing word.
usage: Say it to the host when you reach a function after the start time.
leelaQ: What was the reason you were late the last time?
answer: There was heavy traffic on the main road.

en: It's my fault. I should have called you first.
tamil: என் தப்புதான். நான் முதல்ல உங்களுக்கு போன் பண்ணியிருக்கணும்.
context: Accepting blame after a misunderstanding.
explain: 'Should have' + a verb shows a past mistake or regret.
usage: Use it with family or friends when you accept your mistake honestly.
leelaQ: Is it easy for you to accept your own mistake?
answer: Yes, I think saying sorry quickly is always better.

en: No problem at all, these things happen.
tamil: பிரச்சினையே இல்லை, இதெல்லாம் நடக்கத்தான் செய்யும்.
context: Accepting someone's apology kindly.
explain: This line makes the other person feel relaxed after saying sorry.
usage: Say it when a friend or neighbour apologises for a small mistake.
leelaQ: How do you reply when someone says sorry to you?
answer: I smile and say it is okay, no problem.

en: You look great today. Is that a new saree?
tamil: இன்னைக்கு நீங்க ரொம்ப அழகா இருக்கீங்க. இது புது புடவையா?
context: Complimenting a colleague's dress.
explain: A compliment plus a question is a nice way to start talking.
usage: Use it with a friend or colleague to start the day on a happy note.
leelaQ: What was the last compliment you gave someone?
answer: I told my friend that her new haircut looks nice.

en: Your son is so polite. You have brought him up very well.
tamil: உங்க பையன் ரொம்ப மரியாதையானவன். நீங்க நல்லா வளர்த்திருக்கீங்க.
context: Praising a neighbour's child.
explain: 'Bring up' means to raise a child. 'Have brought up' is present perfect.
usage: Say it to parents when their child behaves well in front of you.
leelaQ: What good habits did your parents teach you?
answer: They taught me to respect elders and speak the truth.

en: Thank you for your kind words, that means a lot to me.
tamil: உங்க அன்பான வார்த்தைகளுக்கு நன்றி, அது எனக்கு ரொம்ப முக்கியம்.
context: Replying to a heartfelt compliment.
explain: 'Means a lot' shows deep feeling and thanks.
usage: Use it after someone praises you or says something touching.
leelaQ: How do you reply when someone praises your work?
answer: I smile and say thank you very much.

en: I really appreciate your help with the shifting.
tamil: வீடு மாத்தறதுல நீங்க செஞ்ச உதவிக்கு ரொம்ப நன்றி.
context: Thanking friends who helped you move house.
explain: 'Appreciate' is a stronger and more formal word than 'like' for thanks.
usage: Say it to friends or neighbours who helped you in a big task.
leelaQ: Who helped you the most in the last month?
answer: My neighbour helped me a lot when I was sick.

en: I owe you one. You saved me today.
tamil: நான் உங்களுக்கு கடமைப்பட்டிருக்கேன். இன்னைக்கு நீங்கதான் என்னைக் காப்பாத்தினீங்க.
context: Thanking a friend after a big favour.
explain: 'I owe you one' means I will return this favour in future.
usage: Use it with close friends or colleagues after they help in an emergency.
leelaQ: When did a friend save you from a problem?
answer: A friend gave me a lift when my bike broke down.

en: You shouldn't have, it's such a beautiful gift!
tamil: இதெல்லாம் வேண்டாமே, எவ்ளோ அழகான பரிசு!
context: Receiving a surprise gift.
explain: 'You shouldn't have' is a polite way to say thank you for a nice gift.
usage: Say it when someone gives you an unexpected present.
leelaQ: What was the best gift you ever received?
answer: The best gift was a watch from my father.

en: Could you pass me the water jug, please?
tamil: தயவு செஞ்சு அந்த தண்ணி ஜக்கை கொஞ்சம் தர்றீங்களா?
context: Asking someone at the dining table.
explain: 'Could you pass me' is a polite way to ask for something at a table.
usage: Use it at a family meal or a function dinner table.
leelaQ: What do you usually drink with your meals?
answer: I usually drink plain water with my meals.

en: Let me help you with those bags.
tamil: அந்த பைகளை தூக்க நான் உதவி பண்றேன்.
context: Offering to carry bags for an elderly neighbour.
explain: 'Let me...' is a simple way to offer help.
usage: Say it to elders, guests or neighbours who are carrying heavy things.
leelaQ: When did you last help an elder person?
answer: I helped my grandmother cross the road yesterday.

en: We have been neighbours for ten years, but we never talk.
tamil: நாம பத்து வருஷமா பக்கத்து வீட்டுக்காரங்க, ஆனா பேசிக்கவே மாட்டோம்.
context: Chatting about a quiet neighbour.
explain: 'Never' makes the sentence negative. 'Have been' shows something that started in the past and continues.
usage: Use it when you talk about people you live near but do not know well.
leelaQ: Do you know your neighbours well?
answer: I know a few of them and we talk on weekends.

en: The new neighbours seem very friendly.
tamil: புது பக்கத்து வீட்டுக்காரங்க ரொம்ப நட்பா தெரியறாங்க.
context: Telling your family about new neighbours.
explain: 'Seem' is used when you form an opinion by looking or listening.
usage: Use it at home or with friends when you speak about new people nearby.
leelaQ: How do you welcome new neighbours?
answer: I take some sweets and say hello to them.

en: Could you please keep the music down after ten?
tamil: பத்து மணிக்கு மேல பாட்டை கொஞ்சம் சத்தம் குறைச்சு வைக்க முடியுமா?
context: Requesting a neighbour politely about noise.
explain: 'Keep the music down' means to lower the volume. 'Could you please' keeps it polite.
usage: Use it with a neighbour when the noise disturbs your sleep or study.
leelaQ: What do you do when the neighbours are very noisy?
answer: I speak to them kindly and ask them to lower the sound.

en: Our building is having a Diwali get-together next Sunday.
tamil: அடுத்த ஞாயிற்றுக்கிழமை எங்க அப்பார்ட்மென்ட்ல தீபாவளி கெட்-டுகெதர் இருக்கு.
context: Telling a friend about a community event.
explain: Present continuous can be used for a planned event in the near future.
usage: Use it to invite friends or tell family about a function in your area.
leelaQ: How do you celebrate festivals with your neighbours?
answer: We share sweets and sit together in the evening.

en: Do you want me to water your plants while you are away?
tamil: நீங்க ஊருல இல்லாதப்ப செடிகளுக்கு நான் தண்ணி ஊத்தணுமா?
context: Offering help to a neighbour going on a trip.
explain: 'Do you want me to...' is a kind way to offer help.
usage: Use it with a neighbour before they leave for a long trip.
leelaQ: What can neighbours do for each other when someone travels?
answer: They can collect the post and watch the house.

en: I'll keep an eye on your house while you're gone.
tamil: நீங்க போயிருக்கும்போது உங்க வீட்டை நான் பாத்துக்கறேன்.
context: Promising a neighbour who is travelling.
explain: 'Keep an eye on' means to watch something carefully.
usage: Say it to a neighbour or friend who is leaving home for some days.
leelaQ: Would you trust a neighbour with your house keys?
answer: Yes, I would trust a neighbour I know well.

en: What time does the wedding start tomorrow?
tamil: நாளைக்கு கல்யாணம் எத்தனை மணிக்கு ஆரம்பிக்கும்?
context: Checking the muhurtham time with a relative.
explain: Use present simple for a fixed schedule or event time.
usage: Ask it to a family member or friend before you go to a wedding.
leelaQ: What time do weddings usually start in your family?
answer: Most weddings start early in the morning.

en: Congratulations to both of you, wishing you a happy married life.
tamil: உங்க ரெண்டு பேருக்கும் வாழ்த்துகள், மகிழ்ச்சியான திருமண வாழ்க்கை அமையட்டும்.
context: Greeting the couple on stage at a wedding.
explain: This is a common wish for a newly married couple.
usage: Say it to the bride and groom when you meet them on the stage.
leelaQ: What do you say to the couple at a wedding?
answer: I say congratulations and wish them a happy life.

en: Don't forget to give the gift to the bride before we leave.
tamil: நாம கிளம்பறதுக்கு முன்னாடி மணப்பொண்ணுக்கு பரிசு குடுக்க மறந்துடாதே.
context: Reminding your husband or friend at a wedding.
explain: 'Don't forget to' + a verb is a common reminder.
usage: Use it with family members before leaving a function.
leelaQ: What gift do you usually give at a wedding?
answer: I usually give a gift set or some money in a cover.

en: The wedding hall was decorated with fresh jasmine flowers.
tamil: கல்யாண மண்டபம் புது மல்லிகைப் பூக்களால அலங்கரிக்கப்பட்டிருந்தது.
context: Describing a wedding to a friend who missed it.
explain: 'Was decorated' is passive: it tells what was done, not who did it.
usage: Use it when you tell someone about a function you attended.
leelaQ: How was the last function you attended?
answer: It was very nice and the food was tasty.

en: Have you had lunch yet, or will you join us?
tamil: மதிய சாப்பாடு சாப்பிட்டீங்களா, இல்ல எங்களோட சேர்றீங்களா?
context: Inviting a relative to eat at a function.
explain: 'Have you had lunch yet?' is a very common greeting in Indian homes.
usage: Use it with relatives or guests at a wedding or family event.
leelaQ: Do you like to eat lunch alone or with others?
answer: I like to eat lunch with my friends.

en: I am really sorry for making you wait so long.
tamil: உங்களை இவ்வளவு நேரம் காத்திருக்க வச்சதுக்கு ரொம்ப மன்னிக்கணும்.
context: Apologising to a friend after being late.
explain: 'Sorry for' is followed by an -ing word. 'Really' adds feeling.
usage: Use it when you reach late to meet a friend or a relative.
leelaQ: What do you say when you reach late to meet someone?
answer: I say sorry and tell them the reason for the delay.

en: Welcome to our home. We are so happy you could come.
tamil: எங்க வீட்டுக்கு வரவேற்கிறோம். நீங்க வந்தது ரொம்ப சந்தோஷம்.
context: Greeting guests arriving for a house-warming.
explain: 'We are happy you could come' shows the guests are valued.
usage: Say it at the door when guests arrive for a function at your house.
leelaQ: How do you feel when guests come to your home?
answer: I feel very happy and a little busy.

en: Congratulations on your new house, it is really spacious.
tamil: புது வீட்டுக்கு வாழ்த்துகள், இது ரொம்ப விசாலமா இருக்கு.
context: Visiting a friend's house-warming ceremony.
explain: 'Spacious' means having a lot of room inside.
usage: Say it to a friend who has just moved into a new home.
leelaQ: What kind of house would you like to live in?
answer: I would like a small house with a garden.

en: Sorry to bother you, but do you have a pen I could borrow?
tamil: தொந்தரவுக்கு மன்னிக்கணும், நான் வாங்கிக்கற மாதிரி உங்ககிட்ட பேனா இருக்கா?
context: Asking a stranger for a pen at a function.
explain: 'Sorry to bother you' is a polite opening before a small request.
usage: Use it with strangers when you need a small favour.
leelaQ: Do you carry a pen with you every day?
answer: Yes, I always keep a pen in my bag.

en: It has been ages since we met! How are you?
tamil: நாம சந்திச்சு பல வருஷமாச்சு! எப்படி இருக்கீங்க?
context: Meeting an old school friend by chance.
explain: 'Ages' means a very long time. It is used in spoken English.
usage: Say it when you unexpectedly meet someone after many years.
leelaQ: Whom did you meet after a long time recently?
answer: I met my school friend at the bus stand.

en: Let's exchange numbers so we can plan a meetup.
tamil: நம்பர் மாத்திக்கலாம், அப்புறம் சந்திக்க திட்டம் போடலாம்.
context: Getting a new friend's phone number.
explain: 'Let's' is used to make a suggestion for both of you.
usage: Use it when you like a new person and want to meet again.
leelaQ: How many contacts do you have on your phone?
answer: I have around two hundred contacts.

en: What kind of work do you do?
tamil: நீங்க என்ன மாதிரி வேலை செய்யறீங்க?
context: Making small talk with a new acquaintance.
explain: 'What kind of' asks about the type of something. It sounds friendly, not pushy.
usage: Ask it casually when you meet someone for the first time.
leelaQ: What kind of work do you do and do you enjoy it?
answer: I work in an office and I enjoy it.

en: I work in a software company near the airport.
tamil: நான் விமான நிலையம் பக்கத்துல ஒரு சாஃப்ட்வேர் கம்பெனியில வேலை பாக்கறேன்.
context: Telling a new person about your job.
explain: 'Work in' is used for a company or field; 'work at' for a place.
usage: Say it when someone asks about your job at a party.
leelaQ: Where is your office and how do you go there?
answer: My office is near the station and I go by bus.

en: You two must come over for tea this evening.
tamil: நீங்க ரெண்டு பேரும் இன்னைக்கு சாயந்திரம் டீக்கு வீட்டுக்கு வரணும்.
context: Inviting neighbours to your home.
explain: 'Come over' means to visit someone's home. 'Must' makes the invitation warm.
usage: Use it to invite close neighbours or friends for a casual visit.
leelaQ: Do you like drinking tea in the evening?
answer: Yes, I always drink tea at five o'clock.

en: We'll definitely come to your daughter's engagement.
tamil: உங்க பொண்ணோட நிச்சயதார்த்தத்துக்கு நிச்சயம் வருவோம்.
context: Accepting an invitation from a colleague.
explain: 'Definitely' shows you are very sure about coming.
usage: Say it to promise a friend or colleague that you will attend.
leelaQ: Do you always keep your promise to attend functions?
answer: Yes, I try my best to attend every function.

en: I'm sorry, we already have another function that day.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், அன்னைக்கு எங்களுக்கு வேற ஒரு விழா இருக்கு.
context: Declining a wedding invitation politely.
explain: Giving a short reason makes a refusal polite.
usage: Say it when you cannot go to a function because of another plan.
leelaQ: What do you do if two functions come on the same day?
answer: I go to the closer relative's function first.

en: Would you mind taking a photo of all of us?
tamil: எங்க எல்லாரையும் ஒரு போட்டோ எடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a stranger to take a group photo.
explain: 'Would you mind...ing' is a very polite request form.
usage: Use it with strangers at a tourist place or a function.
leelaQ: Do you like taking photos at functions?
answer: Yes, I love taking photos with my family.

en: Everyone loved your speech at the reception.
tamil: வரவேற்புல நீங்க பேசினது எல்லாருக்கும் ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருந்துச்சு.
context: Praising a friend after his speech.
explain: 'Loved' is a stronger word than 'liked'.
usage: Say it to a person who spoke on stage and did well.
leelaQ: Can you speak confidently in front of a crowd?
answer: Not yet, but I am practising every day.

en: Thank you for coming all the way from Chennai.
tamil: சென்னையில இருந்து இவ்வளவு தூரம் வந்ததுக்கு நன்றி.
context: Thanking a relative who travelled far.
explain: 'All the way' stresses the long distance someone travelled.
usage: Say it to guests who have made a long trip for your function.
leelaQ: Which relative lives very far from your home?
answer: My uncle lives in Bangalore, very far from us.

en: I didn't recognise you at first. You've changed so much!
tamil: எனக்கு முதல்ல உங்களை அடையாளமே தெரியலை. நீங்க ரொம்ப மாறிட்டீங்க!
context: Meeting someone after many years.
explain: 'Recognise' means to know someone from before.
usage: Use it with old friends or relatives you meet after a long gap.
leelaQ: Has any friend of yours changed a lot over the years?
answer: Yes, my friend became much slimmer and more confident.

en: Make sure you give my regards to your parents.
tamil: உங்க அம்மா அப்பாகிட்ட என் வணக்கத்தை சொல்லுங்க.
context: Saying goodbye to a friend.
explain: 'Give my regards to' is a polite way to send greetings.
usage: Say it at the end of a chat when you want to greet someone's family.
leelaQ: How are your parents and what do they do?
answer: They are fine and they enjoy gardening.

en: Are you enjoying the party so far?
tamil: இதுவரைக்கும் பார்ட்டியை எஞ்சாய் பண்றீங்களா?
context: Checking on a guest at your party.
explain: 'So far' means until now.
usage: Ask it to a guest to show care as a host.
leelaQ: What do you enjoy most at a party?
answer: I enjoy the music and meeting new people.

en: I'm new to this city, so I don't know many people yet.
tamil: நான் இந்த ஊருக்கு புதுசு, அதனால இன்னும் நிறைய பேரை தெரியாது.
context: Telling a friendly colleague about yourself.
explain: 'Yet' is used in negatives to mean 'until now'.
usage: Use it to explain why you are alone when you move to a new place.
leelaQ: How do you make friends in a new city?
answer: I join a club and talk to my neighbours.

en: Let me introduce my friend Priya, she's visiting from Coimbatore.
tamil: என் தோழி பிரியாவை அறிமுகப்படுத்தறேன், அவ கோயம்புத்தூர்ல இருந்து வந்திருக்கா.
context: Introducing a friend to your colleagues.
explain: 'Let me introduce' is a formal and polite way to bring in a new person.
usage: Use it when you bring a friend to a group of people.
leelaQ: Who did you introduce to your family last?
answer: I introduced my best friend to my parents.

en: I was so nervous about meeting her parents for the first time.
tamil: அவளோட அம்மா அப்பாவை முதல் தடவை பாக்க எனக்கு ரொம்ப பதட்டமா இருந்துச்சு.
context: Telling a friend about a nervous experience.
explain: 'Nervous about' + an -ing word shows worry about a future event.
usage: Say it when you share your feelings about a big meeting.
leelaQ: What makes you nervous when you meet new people?
answer: I get nervous when I have to speak first.

en: Please accept this small gift as a token of my thanks.
tamil: என் நன்றியோட அடையாளமா இந்த சின்ன பரிசை ஏத்துக்கோங்க.
context: Giving a gift to someone who helped you.
explain: 'A token of' means a small sign of a feeling.
usage: Say it when you hand over a thank-you gift to a helper or teacher.
leelaQ: Whom would you like to give a thank-you gift?
answer: I would like to thank my teacher with a gift.

en: My family is going to visit your village next month.
tamil: என் குடும்பம் அடுத்த மாசம் உங்க கிராமத்துக்கு வரப்போறோம்.
context: Telling a friend about a planned visit.
explain: 'Going to' is used for plans you have already decided.
usage: Say it to a friend or relative when you plan to meet them.
leelaQ: Which village or town would you like to visit?
answer: I would like to visit a hill station in the summer.

en: What a lovely surprise! I never expected to see you here.
tamil: என்ன ஒரு இனிய ஆச்சரியம்! உங்களை இங்க பாப்பேன்னு நான் நினைக்கவே இல்லை.
context: Meeting a friend unexpectedly in a mall.
explain: 'Never expected' shows complete surprise. 'What a...' shows strong feeling.
usage: Use it when you meet a known person in an unexpected place.
leelaQ: Have you ever met a friend in a surprising place?
answer: Yes, I once met my cousin at the airport.

en: Do join us if you are free this Sunday.
tamil: இந்த ஞாயிற்றுக்கிழமை உங்களுக்கு நேரமிருந்தா எங்களோட சேருங்க.
context: Giving a casual invite to a neighbour.
explain: 'Do' before a verb makes a request warm and strong.
usage: Use it to invite someone in a friendly, no-pressure way.
leelaQ: What do you usually do on Sunday?
answer: I relax at home and meet my friends.

en: That is a lovely saree. The colour suits you very well.
tamil: அது அழகான புடவை. அந்த நிறம் உங்களுக்கு ரொம்ப பொருத்தமா இருக்கு.
context: Complimenting a relative at a wedding.
explain: 'Suits you' means looks good on you. It is a polite way to praise someone.
usage: Say it to a woman at a wedding or festival to praise her dress.
leelaQ: Whose dress did you praise at the last function?
answer: I praised my cousin's saree at her friend's wedding.

en: We are inviting everyone for my sister's engagement next Sunday.
tamil: அடுத்த ஞாயிற்றுக்கிழமை என் தங்கை நிச்சயதார்த்தத்துக்கு எல்லாரையும் கூப்பிடறோம்.
context: Inviting a neighbour to a family function.
explain: Present continuous with 'next Sunday' talks about a planned event.
usage: Use it when you personally invite neighbours or friends to a family event.
leelaQ: Who will you invite to the next family function?
answer: I will invite my neighbours and close friends.

en: Many thanks for the lovely evening, we really enjoyed it.
tamil: அருமையான சாயந்திரத்துக்கு ரொம்ப நன்றி, நாங்க ரொம்ப ரசிச்சோம்.
context: Thanking a host while leaving.
explain: This sentence thanks the host and says you enjoyed the time.
usage: Say it at the door when you are leaving a dinner or a get-together.
leelaQ: What was the last evening you really enjoyed?
answer: I enjoyed a family dinner last Sunday.

en: You have a beautiful smile, it lights up the room.
tamil: உங்க சிரிப்பு ரொம்ப அழகு, அது அறையையே பிரகாசமாக்கும்.
context: Complimenting a friend kindly.
explain: 'Light up' is used for something that makes a place feel bright and happy.
usage: Use it with a close friend or family member in a warm moment.
leelaQ: Who has the nicest smile among your friends?
answer: My best friend has the nicest smile.

en: Sorry, I spilled some juice on the carpet. I'll clean it right away.
tamil: மன்னிச்சிடுங்க, கார்ப்பெட்ல ஜூஸ் சிந்திடுச்சு. உடனே சுத்தம் பண்றேன்.
context: Apologising to a host for an accident.
explain: Say sorry first, then offer to fix the problem.
usage: Say it to the host at a party when something spills or breaks.
leelaQ: What accident have you had at someone's house?
answer: I once broke a glass at my friend's house.

en: Does anyone here know where the restroom is?
tamil: இங்க யாருக்காவது கழிவறை எங்க இருக்குன்னு தெரியுமா?
context: Asking guests at a big function.
explain: 'Restroom' is a polite word for toilet.
usage: Ask it in a wedding hall or a big party when you cannot find the place.
leelaQ: What do you do when you are lost in a new place?
answer: I ask a person nearby or use the map on my phone.

en: My sister is getting married in December, and you're all invited.
tamil: என் தங்கச்சிக்கு டிசம்பர்ல கல்யாணம், நீங்க எல்லாரும் வரணும்.
context: Inviting colleagues to a family wedding.
explain: 'Getting married' with a future time shows a planned event.
usage: Say it to colleagues or friends when you share a wedding news.
leelaQ: Who is getting married in your family soon?
answer: My cousin is getting married next year.

en: I'd love to come, but I have to check with my wife first.
tamil: நான் வர ஆசைப்படறேன், ஆனா முதல்ல என் மனைவிகிட்ட கேக்கணும்.
context: Giving a soft answer to an invitation.
explain: 'I'd love to, but...' accepts warmly and keeps a small condition.
usage: Use it when you want to attend but you need to confirm your plan.
leelaQ: Do you ask your family before accepting invites?
answer: Yes, I always check with my family first.

en: Please don't mention it, it was my pleasure.
tamil: அதை சொல்லாதீங்க, அது எனக்கு சந்தோஷம்தான்.
context: Replying to someone's thanks.
explain: 'My pleasure' is a warm and polite reply to thanks.
usage: Say it when someone thanks you for a small or big help.
leelaQ: How do you reply when someone says thank you?
answer: I say you're welcome or my pleasure.

en: Can I have your attention for a moment, please?
tamil: ஒரு நிமிஷம் எல்லாரும் கவனிக்க முடியுமா, தயவு செஞ்சு?
context: Starting a toast or announcement at a party.
explain: 'Can I have your attention' is a polite way to make a group quiet.
usage: Use it before an announcement at a gathering or family function.
leelaQ: Have you ever made an announcement in a group?
answer: Yes, I did it once at my college farewell.

en: Let's raise a toast to the happy couple.
tamil: மகிழ்ச்சியான தம்பதிகளுக்காக ஒரு வாழ்த்து சொல்லலாம்.
context: Giving a toast at a reception.
explain: 'Raise a toast' means to lift a glass and give good wishes.
usage: Say it at a wedding reception or an anniversary party.
leelaQ: What wishes would you give to a newly married couple?
answer: I would wish them love, health and happiness.

en: You've been so kind to us since we moved here.
tamil: நாங்க இங்க வந்ததுல இருந்து நீங்க எங்ககிட்ட ரொம்ப அன்பா இருக்கீங்க.
context: Thanking a neighbour who helped the new family.
explain: 'Since' + a past event shows the start of a time up to now.
usage: Say it to a neighbour who has been helping you for a while.
leelaQ: What is the kindest thing a neighbour did for you?
answer: A neighbour gave us food when we moved in.

en: I'm sorry for the misunderstanding, I should have explained it better.
tamil: தப்பா புரிஞ்சதுக்கு மன்னிக்கணும், நான் இன்னும் நல்லா விளக்கியிருக்கணும்.
context: Apologising to a friend after a confusion.
explain: 'Should have explained' admits that you could have done better.
usage: Use it with friends or colleagues to clear a confusion calmly.
leelaQ: Have you ever had a misunderstanding with a friend?
answer: Yes, but we talked and solved it quickly.

en: Please stay for dinner. It is no trouble at all.
tamil: தயவு செஞ்சு டின்னர் சாப்பிட்டுட்டு போங்க. எந்த சிரமமும் இல்லை.
context: Inviting a visiting friend to eat.
explain: 'Please stay' is a warm invitation. 'No trouble' tells the guest they are welcome.
usage: Use it when a friend visits near meal time.
leelaQ: What do you cook when a friend visits suddenly?
answer: I make dosa or rice with some curry.

en: Sorry, I can't hear you, the music is too loud.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், எனக்கு கேக்கலை, பாட்டு ரொம்ப சத்தமா இருக்கு.
context: Talking in a noisy party.
explain: 'Too loud' means more loud than you can bear.
usage: Say it at a party or a wedding with loud music.
leelaQ: Do you like loud music at parties?
answer: No, I prefer soft music so we can talk.

en: We should do this more often, it was a great get-together.
tamil: இதை அடிக்கடி செய்யணும், இது நல்ல கெட்-டுகெதர்.
context: Saying goodbye after a friends' meet.
explain: 'We should' is used to give a gentle suggestion to a group.
usage: Say it at the end of a friends' meet or family gathering.
leelaQ: How often do you meet your old friends?
answer: We meet once in three months.

en: My neighbour's daughter won a gold medal in the state meet.
tamil: என் பக்கத்து வீட்டு பொண்ணு மாநில போட்டியில தங்க பதக்கம் வாங்கினா.
context: Sharing good news about a neighbour.
explain: 'Won' is the past form of 'win'.
usage: Say it at home or with friends when you share happy local news.
leelaQ: Do you know anyone who won a prize recently?
answer: Yes, my friend won a prize in a quiz.

en: Aunty, please have a seat. I'll get you some water.
tamil: ஆன்டி, உட்காருங்க. நான் உங்களுக்கு தண்ணி கொண்டு வரேன்.
context: Welcoming an elderly visitor politely.
explain: 'Have a seat' is a polite way to say 'please sit'.
usage: Use it with elders who visit your home or office.
leelaQ: How do you show respect to elders?
answer: I greet them, offer a seat and speak politely.

en: Thank you for remembering my birthday, that was so sweet of you.
tamil: என் பிறந்தநாளை நினைவு வெச்சதுக்கு நன்றி, ரொம்ப அன்பான செயல்.
context: Thanking a friend for a birthday wish.
explain: 'So sweet of you' means very kind and thoughtful.
usage: Say it to anyone who sends a wish or a message on your special day.
leelaQ: Who wished you first on your last birthday?
answer: My mother wished me first at midnight.

en: If you need anything, just call me.
tamil: உங்களுக்கு ஏதாவது வேணும்னா, எனக்கு போன் பண்ணுங்க.
context: Offering support to a neighbour or friend.
explain: This is a first-conditional style offer: if + present, then an instruction.
usage: Say it to a friend or neighbour who is in a difficult time.
leelaQ: When did you last help a friend in need?
answer: I helped my friend find a house last month.

en: Is this your first time in Madurai?
tamil: நீங்க மதுரைக்கு வர்றது இதுதான் முதல் தடவையா?
context: Talking to a tourist at a temple.
explain: 'Is this your first time in...?' is a common way to chat with visitors.
usage: Ask it to a visitor or tourist to start a friendly chat.
leelaQ: Which new city did you visit the last time?
answer: I visited Pondicherry last year.

en: I've never been to a destination wedding before.
tamil: நான் இதுவரைக்கும் டெஸ்டினேஷன் வெடிங்குக்கு போனதே இல்லை.
context: Chatting about an upcoming wedding.
explain: 'Never...before' with 'have' talks about life experience.
usage: Say it when you speak about a new or first-time experience.
leelaQ: What is a new thing you want to try soon?
answer: I want to try scuba diving soon.

en: Congratulations, you must be so proud of your daughter.
tamil: வாழ்த்துகள், உங்க பொண்ணை நினைச்சு நீங்க ரொம்ப பெருமைப்படுவீங்க.
context: Greeting a parent after a child's success.
explain: 'Must be' is used when you are sure about someone's feeling.
usage: Say it to parents when their child gets a prize or a job.
leelaQ: What makes your parents feel proud of you?
answer: They feel proud when I do well in my job.

en: I'll see you at the temple festival next week.
tamil: அடுத்த வாரம் கோயில் திருவிழாவுல பாக்கலாம்.
context: Saying goodbye to a friend.
explain: 'I'll see you at' is a common way to say goodbye when you plan to meet.
usage: Use it when you say bye to someone you will meet soon.
leelaQ: Which festival do you enjoy the most?
answer: I enjoy Pongal the most because of the food.

en: It's a pleasure to meet you, sir. Thank you for your time.
tamil: உங்களை சந்திச்சது எனக்கு மகிழ்ச்சி சார். உங்க நேரத்துக்கு நன்றி.
context: Meeting an important person politely.
explain: 'It's a pleasure to meet you' is more formal than 'nice to meet you'.
usage: Use it with senior people, elders or officials you meet for the first time.
leelaQ: How do you greet a person older than you?
answer: I greet them with a smile and say good morning.

en: Please say hello to your family from all of us.
tamil: எங்க எல்லார் சார்பாகவும் உங்க குடும்பத்துக்கு ஹலோ சொல்லுங்க.
context: Ending a phone call with a friend.
explain: This is a friendly line to send greetings through someone.
usage: Use it at the end of a call or visit to greet someone's family.
leelaQ: Who do you talk to on the phone every day?
answer: I talk to my mother every evening.

en: Please do not mind, I cannot come to the party this time.
tamil: தப்பா எடுத்துக்காதீங்க, இந்த தடவை பார்ட்டிக்கு என்னால வர முடியாது.
context: Politely declining an invitation.
explain: 'Do not mind' softens a refusal. 'Cannot' tells you are unable to do it.
usage: Use it with a friend when you must refuse an invitation politely.
leelaQ: How do you refuse an invitation politely?
answer: I say thank you and give a short reason.
